wiki/content/quaternionic-analysis/fuete.content: --- title: Fueter regularity and discrete series description: Weighted regular spinors, explicit group actions, compact types, and proofs of irreducibility and square-integrability. section: Quaternionic analysis article-kind: exposition order: 4 --- # Fueter regularity and discrete series :::discussion Fueter regularity realizes an entire family of discrete-series representations when the coefficients are compatible symmetric spinors. The construction below gives the Hilbert spaces, the group action, and the proofs. The case of one unrestricted quaternionic value is the Hardy limit discussed in the following article. ::: ## The group and its coefficient spaces Put $G=\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)$, $K=\operatorname{Sp}(1)_L\times\operatorname{Sp}(1)_R$, $B=\{q\in\mathbb H:|q|<1\}$, and $s(q)=1-|q|^2$. Explicitly $G=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb H):g^*\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)g=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\}$, where $g^*$ is conjugate transpose. Its action is $gq=(aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1}$ and $K$ consists of $\operatorname{diag}(a,b)$ with $|a|=|b|=1$. All representations and Hilbert spaces below are complex. For quaternion coefficients, the complex scalar acts on the right. Let $V_n=\mathbb C[X,Y]_n$ with $$ (\tau_n(M)p)(X,Y)=p(aX+cY,bX+dY),\qquad M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}, $$ and the norm $$ \left\|\sum_{k=0}^n c_kX^{n-k}Y^k\right\|_n^2 =\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{|c_k|^2}{\binom nk}. $$ A quaternion acts through $$ \iota(t+ix+jy+kz)=\begin{pmatrix}t+ix&y+iz\\-y+iz&t-ix\end{pmatrix}. $$ Write a quaternion-valued homogeneous polynomial of auxiliary degree $n-1$ as $$ h(q;X,Y)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}h_k(q)X^{n-1-k}Y^k=A(q;X,Y)-jB(q;X,Y), $$ where $A,B$ have complex coefficients. Auxiliary variables commute with quaternion coefficients. For $n\ge1$, put $$ W_n=\{A-jB:A_Y=B_X\}\subset\mathbb H[X,Y]_{n-1}. \tag{C1} $$ Here $A,B\in\mathbb C[X,Y]_{n-1}$; we refer to $A_Y=B_X$ as the compatibility condition. The first compact factor acts trivially on $V_n$. Let $T_np=p_X-jp_Y$ and $\mathcal T_n=T_n/n$ for $n\ge1$. For a quaternion coefficient row of length $n$, use the squared norm $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|h_k|^2/\binom{n-1}{k}$; the auxiliary variables $X,Y$ commute with coefficients. Write $D_l=\partial_t+i\partial_x+j\partial_y+k\partial_z$, coefficientwise, with $x=x_1,y=x_2,z=x_3$ in the foundations article. The compatibility condition is imposed pointwise for functions of $q$. Proposition [DS1](#ds1) identifies $W_n$ with $V_n$ and proves that its complex dimension is $n+1$. ::::proposition DS1 | The spinor-to-Fueter isometry Version: 1 Uses: [Spinor conventions](#spinor-conventions), [coefficient model](#ds-d1). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $n\ge1$, $\mathcal T_n:V_n\to W_n$ is a complex-linear isometric isomorphism, with inverse $A-jB\mapsto XA+YB$. In particular $\dim_{\mathbb C}W_n=n+1$. :::proof Proof of DS1 The polynomials $f_X/n$ and $f_Y/n$ satisfy the compatibility condition, and for $h=A-jB\in W_n$ the inverse is particularly simple: $$ \mathcal T_n^{-1}h=XA+YB. \tag{C5} $$ Differentiating (C5), using $A_Y=B_X$ and Euler's identity, gives $(XA+YB)_X=nA$ and $(XA+YB)_Y=nB$. This proves the inverse formula. For a monomial $X^{n-k}Y^k$, the squared norm of $T_n$'s image is $$ \frac{(n-k)^2}{\binom{n-1}{k}}+ \frac{k^2}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}} =\frac{n^2}{\binom nk}, $$ with absent endpoint terms omitted. Images of distinct monomials are orthogonal for the underlying complex inner product, proving the isometry. ::: :::: ## Weighted Hilbert spaces and the action Use Euclidean volume $dv=dt\,dx\,dy\,dz$ on $B$. ::::definition DS-D2 | Weighted Regular Functions Version: 1 Uses: [Spinor conventions](#spinor-conventions), [coefficient model](#ds-d1), [DS1](#ds1). --- For an integer $n\ge2$, put $C_n=n(n-1)/\pi^2$. The **weighted regular space** consists of the smooth functions in $$ \mathcal H_n=\left\{h:B\longrightarrow W_n: D_lh=0,\quad \|h\|_{\mathcal H_n}^2 =C_n\int_B\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{|h_k(q)|^2}{\binom{n-1}{k}} s(q)^{n-2}\,dv(q)<\infty\right\}, \tag{C2} $$ where $D_l=\partial_t+i\partial_x+j\partial_y+k\partial_z$ acts coefficientwise. :::: The polynomial-spinor model is $$ \mathcal B_n=\{f\in L^2(B,V_n,d\mu_n):D_l(T_nf)=0\},\quad d\mu_n=C_ns^{n-2}dv.\tag{C6} $$ Here the equation is imposed distributionally. The map $\mathcal T_n$ identifies $\mathcal B_n$ isometrically with $\mathcal H_n$ by [DS1](#ds1); smoothness of the distributional kernels is proved in [DS2](#ds2). The measure $\mu_n$ has total mass one, since polar coordinates give $$ \int_Bs^{n-2}dv =2\pi^2\int_0^1r^3(1-r^2)^{n-2}\,dr =\frac{\pi^2}{n(n-1)}. $$ For $\gamma\in G$, write $$ \gamma^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad q'=(aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1},\qquad J=cq+d. $$ Let $S_m(M)$ be the coefficient-column matrix of $\tau_m(M)$ in descending monomials; in particular $S_1(M)=M$. Regard $h=(h_0,\ldots,h_{n-1})$ as a row. ::::construction DS-C1 | The Möbius Representation Version: 1 Uses: [Spinor conventions](#spinor-conventions), [coefficient model](#ds-d1), [DS-D2](#ds-d2). Justification: The group law, covariance, and unitarity in [DS2](#ds2). Origin: consequence --- Define $$ \boxed{(\Pi_n(\gamma)h)(q) =|J|^{-2}J^{-1}h(q')\,S_{n-1}(\iota(J^{-1}))^t.} \tag{C3} $$ The matrix entries multiply quaternion coefficients on the right, while $J^{-1}$ multiplies on the left. On polynomial spinors the corresponding formula is $$ (\pi_n(\gamma)f)(q)=|J|^{-2}\tau_n(J^{-1})f(q').\tag{C7} $$ :::: ::::theorem DS2 | Completeness, covariance, and unitarity Version: 1 Uses: [DS1](#ds1), [DS-D2](#ds-d2), [DS-C1](#ds-c1), [SC3](spinor-connection.md#sc3). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: consequence --- For $n\ge2$, $\mathcal H_n$ and $\mathcal B_n$ are nonzero complete Hilbert spaces. Their distributional kernels have smooth harmonic representatives. The formulas in DS-C1 define strongly continuous unitary group representations, and $\mathcal T_n\pi_n=\Pi_n\mathcal T_n$. :::proof Proof of DS2 The Schmid-kernel realization is [[1, eq. (2.8), Prop. 3.6]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012); [SC3](spinor-connection.md#sc3) gives its expression in the present frame. If $D_l(T_nf)=0$ distributionally, apply $\overline D_l=\partial_t-i\partial_x-j\partial_y-k\partial_z$. Since $\overline D_lD_l=\Delta$ and $T_n$ is a fixed injective linear map, $\Delta f=0$ distributionally. Weyl's lemma gives a smooth harmonic representative. In particular all its coefficient functions are harmonic. For a convergent sequence in the weighted $L^2$ norm, convergence also holds in $L^2$ on each compact subset, because the weight is strictly positive there. The distributional equation passes to the limit, as does the fixed algebraic fibre constraint. Consequently (C6) is closed and complete. Interior harmonic estimates make evaluation at each point continuous. This also justifies differentiating and averaging its vectors inside the ball. Quaternion arguments of $\tau_n$ always mean their $\iota$ matrices. The cocycle $J(g_1g_2,q)=J(g_1,g_2q)J(g_2,q)$ proves the group law with the indicated inverse-element convention. The polynomial chain rule shows $$ \mathcal T_n\pi_n(\gamma)=\Pi_n(\gamma)\mathcal T_n, $$ including the inverse and transpose in (C3). For covariance of the differential equation, lift $f$ to $$ F_f(g)=|d|^{-2}\tau_n(d^{-1})f(g\cdot0),\qquad g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}. \tag{C8} $$ Here the blocks belong to $g$, not its inverse. This is a right-K-equivariant function, $F_f(gk)=\tau_n(k_R)^{-1}F_f(g)$. The [connection and weight theorem](spinor-connection.md#sc3) establishes $$ 24(\mathscr DF_f)(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+4)/2}D_l(T_nf),\qquad F_f(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2}f(q). \tag{C9} $$ Left translation on the lifted space commutes with $\mathscr D$, so it preserves the kernel and gives (C7). The connection and its curvature are included in that calculation. For unitarity, write $r=|J|$. Then $$ s(q')=s(q)/r^2,\qquad dv(q')=r^{-8}dv(q),\qquad \||J|^{-2}\tau_n(J^{-1})v\|^2=r^{-2n-4}\|v\|^2. $$ These factors cancel exactly against the weight $s^{n-2}$ in the change of variables. Hence (C7), and therefore (C3), are unitary. Strong continuity follows first on compactly supported continuous functions in the ambient weighted $L^2$ space by change of variables, then by density and unitarity; the closed invariant kernel inherits it. Nonzeroness follows from the constant $V_n$-valued functions. ::: :::: ## Irreducibility and discrete series ::::theorem DS3 | Irreducibility by compact averaging Version: 1 Uses: [DS2](#ds2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: consequence --- For each $n\ge2$, the representation on $\mathcal B_n$, equivalently on $\mathcal H_n$, is irreducible. The group translates of the constant $V_n$ have dense span. :::proof Proof of DS3 The compact action is $$ (\pi_n(a,b)f)(q)=\tau_n(b)f(a^{-1}qb). \tag{C10} $$ Average over the first factor, with Haar probability measure: $$ (P_Lf)(q)=\int_{\operatorname{Sp}(1)}f(a^{-1}q)\,da=f(0). \tag{C11} $$ For $q\ne0$, this is the spherical mean of the harmonic function $f$ over the sphere of radius $|q|$; for $q=0$ it is immediate. Thus $P_L$ is the orthogonal projection onto the constant $V_n$. The second compact factor acts irreducibly on those constants by $\tau_n$. Let $M$ be a nonzero closed $G$-invariant subspace. Choose $f\in M$ and a point $p$ with $f(p)\ne0$. Transitivity and the invertible fibre multiplier give a translate $\pi_n(g)f$ nonzero at $0$. Averaging that vector by $P_L$ gives a nonzero constant in $M$. Its second-compact-factor orbit spans the entire constant $V_n$, so $M$ contains every constant. If $M$ were proper, unitarity would make $M^\perp$ another nonzero closed invariant subspace. The same argument would put all constants in $M^\perp$, a contradiction. Therefore the representation is irreducible. Equivalently, the translates of its constant $V_n$ span a dense subspace. ::: :::: ::::theorem DS4 | A closed embedding into the regular representation Version: 1 Uses: [DS2](#ds2), [DS3](#ds3). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: consequence --- For $n\ge2$, the representation belongs to the discrete series of $\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)$. For any nonzero $v\in V_n$, let $c_v$ be its constant function and put $(\mathcal W_vf)(g)=\langle\pi_n(g^{-1})f,c_v\rangle$, with inner product linear in the first argument. This map has closed image in $L^2(G)$ and satisfies $$ \|\mathcal W_vf\|_{L^2(G)}^2=\frac{\|v\|^2}{(n+1)C_n}\|f\|_{\mathcal B_n}^2 $$ for the Haar measure specified in the proof. :::proof Proof of DS4 Fix Haar measure by $$ \int_G\Phi(g)\,dg=\int_B\int_K\Phi(\sigma(q)k)\,dk\,s(q)^{-4}dv(q), \qquad \int_Kdk=1 $$ in this disintegration convention. The base measure is invariant. Let $v\in V_n$ be nonzero and $c_v$ its constant function. Use a complex inner product linear in the first argument. Harmonic mean values and the probability measure give $$ \langle f,c_v\rangle_{\mathcal B_n}=\langle f(0),v\rangle_{V_n}. $$ The matrix-coefficient map $$ (\mathcal W_vf)(g) =\langle\pi_n(g^{-1})f,c_v\rangle =\langle F_f(g),v\rangle \tag{C12} $$ intertwines $\pi_n$ with left translation on functions on $G$. Schur orthogonality for the finite-dimensional irreducible $\tau_n$ gives $$ \int_K|\langle\tau_n(k_R)^{-1}u,v\rangle|^2dk =\frac{\|u\|^2\|v\|^2}{n+1}. $$ Since $F_f(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2}f(q)$, we obtain the exact norm identity $$ \boxed{\|\mathcal W_vf\|_{L^2(G)}^2 =\frac{\|v\|^2}{(n+1)C_n}\,\|f\|_{\mathcal B_n}^2.} \tag{C13} $$ Thus a fixed scalar multiple of $\mathcal W_v$ is an isometric embedding with closed invariant image in $L^2(G)$. Together with irreducibility, this proves that $\mathcal B_n$ and $\mathcal H_n$ are discrete series. For normalized $v$, the inverse constant in (C13) is $n(n^2-1)/\pi^2$ for the specified Haar measure. Its vanishing at the endpoint is consistent with the divergence proved in [H4](fueter-hardy-space.md#h4); it is not used as a substitute for that argument. ::: :::: ## Compact types and explicit vectors ::::theorem DS5 | The complete compact decomposition Version: 1 Uses: [DS2](#ds2), Clebsch–Gordan and spherical harmonic decomposition. Review: pending Formal: none Origin: literature Cite: [[1, Thms. 3.9, 3.11]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012) --- For $n\ge2$, $$ \mathcal H_n|_K\simeq\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m\ge0}V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n}. $$ Every type occurs once. Coordinate degree $m$ has dimension $(m+1)(m+n+1)$, and the constants form the unique minimal type $V_0\boxtimes V_n$. The same polynomial-kernel calculation holds for $n=1$ and supplies the compact types of the Hardy space. :::proof Proof of DS5 Let $\mathcal P_{m,n}$ be the degree-$m$ homogeneous polynomials in the real coordinates of $q$, valued in $V_n$, satisfying $D_l(T_nf)=0$. Harmonicity puts this space inside $$ \mathrm{SH}_m(\mathbb R^4)\otimes V_n \simeq V_m\boxtimes(V_m\otimes V_n). $$ Here the scalar spherical harmonics on $S^3\simeq\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ carry the standard left/right type $V_m\boxtimes V_m$. For the right factor set $R_jf=\partial_{qe_j}f$, where $e_0=1,e_1=i,e_2=j,e_3=k$. On degree-$m$ functions $R_0=mI$. The infinitesimal action is $d\tau_n(e_j)+R_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, so its Casimir is $$ C_R=-n(n+2)-m(m+2)+2\sum_{j=1}^3d\tau_n(e_j)R_j. $$ The equation forces the cross term to be $-mn$. To check this without an implicit coordinate change, put $\mathbf Tf=(f_X,f_Y)^t$ and write the flat equation as $$ \sum_{i=0}^3\iota(e_i)\mathbf T(\partial_if)=0. $$ Multiply on the left by $\iota(\bar q)$ and contract a column $(A,B)^t$ to $XA+YB$. The result is $$ 0=\sum_i d\tau_n(\bar qe_i)\partial_if =\sum_{j=0}^3d\tau_n(e_j)R_jf. \tag{C14} $$ The last equality follows from $\bar qe_i=\sum_j\langle qe_j,e_i\rangle e_j$. The $j=0$ term is $nmf$, proving the assertion. Consequently $C_R$ acts as $$ -(m+n)(m+n+2). $$ The Clebsch–Gordan decomposition of $V_m\otimes V_n$ has distinct Casimir values and contains $V_{m+n}$ once. Hence $\mathcal P_{m,n}$ lies in $V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n}$. It is nonzero: the explicit seed $$ f_m(q;X,Y)=(t+ix)^mX^n \tag{C15} $$ is regular, because $(\partial_t+i\partial_x)(t+ix)^m=0$. Since the candidate compact summand is irreducible and the kernel is $K$-invariant, its nonzero subspace is the whole summand. Thus $$ \mathcal P_{m,n}=V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n},\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}\mathcal P_{m,n}=(m+1)(m+n+1). $$ Harmonic functions on the ball have homogeneous harmonic expansions. Their degrees are orthogonal on every sphere, and therefore for the radial measure $d\mu_n$. The flat first-order equation holds separately on each homogeneous term. Parseval's identity on spheres and integration in the radius show that partial sums converge in the Hilbert norm. This proves the complete direct-sum decomposition in the theorem. ::: :::: ::::proposition DS6 | Polynomial seeds and translated constants Version: 1 Uses: [DS1](#ds1), [DS3](#ds3), [DS5](#ds5). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $n\ge2$ and $m\ge0$, the vectors $h_m=(t+ix)^mX^{n-1}$ span each compact type under $K$, have squared norm $m!/(n+1)_m$, and the translates of constant spinors displayed in the proof have dense span. :::proof Proof of DS6 Under $\mathcal T_n$, the seed becomes the particularly simple quaternion-valued polynomial $$ h_m(q;X,Y)=(t+ix)^mX^{n-1}. $$ Its squared norm is $$ \|h_m\|^2=\frac{m!}{(n+1)_m},\qquad (n+1)_m=(n+1)(n+2)\cdots(n+m), \tag{C16} $$ by the beta integral. Its $K$-orbit spans the entire type of degree $m$. Constants ($m=0$) are the minimal type; the two highest-weight labels increase with $m$, also making this the unique minimum for the usual compact highest-weight norm. An additional supply of nonpolynomial examples comes directly from translated constants. For any $p\in B$ and $v\in V_n$, $$ f_{p,v}(q)=s(p)^{(n+2)/2}|1-\bar pq|^{-2} \tau_n((1-\bar pq)^{-1})v =\pi_n(\sigma(p))c_v(q). \tag{C17} $$ These are regular spinors of norm $\|v\|$, and $\mathcal T_nf_{p,v}$ are corresponding Fueter-regular vectors. Their span is dense by DS3. For the norm, put $u=t^2+x^2$ and $v=y^2+z^2$. Euclidean measure becomes $\pi^2du\,dv$ after angular integration, so $$ C_n\pi^2\int_{u+v<1}u^m(1-u-v)^{n-2}du\,dv =\frac{m!\,n!}{(m+n)!}. $$ For a translate, $\sigma(p)^{-1}$ has $c=-\bar p/\sqrt{s(p)}$ and $d=1/\sqrt{s(p)}$; substituting these blocks in C7 gives the displayed formula, and unitarity gives its norm. ::: :::: ::::corollary DS7 | The first member as a pair of regular functions Version: 1 Uses: [DS1](#ds1), [DS2](#ds2), [DS5](#ds5), [DS6](#ds6). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- The $n=2$ representation is the space of pairs $(h_0,h_1)=(a-jb,b-jc)$, with $a,b,c$ complex functions on $B$, satisfying coefficientwise Fueter regularity and $$ \|h\|^2=\frac2{\pi^2}\int_B(|h_0|^2+|h_1|^2)\,dv<\infty. $$ Its minimal compact type has complex dimension three. :::proof Proof of DS7 For $n=2$, write $$ f=a(q)X^2+2b(q)XY+c(q)Y^2,\qquad h=\mathcal T_2f=(a-jb)X+(b-jc)Y, $$ where $a,b,c$ are complex-valued. Thus the representation consists exactly of pairs $$ (h_0,h_1)=(a-jb,\ b-jc) $$ that are componentwise Fueter-regular and satisfy $$ \|h\|^2=\frac2{\pi^2}\int_B(|h_0|^2+|h_1|^2)\,dv<\infty. $$ The measure is ordinary ball volume, up to normalization. The action is fully explicit: $$ (\Pi_2(\gamma)h)(q)=|J|^{-2}J^{-1}(h_0(q'),h_1(q'))\iota(J^{-1})^t. $$ Constant pairs of this form constitute the three-dimensional complex minimal $K$-type. The pair $(t+ix,0)$ is a nonconstant vector, of squared norm $1/3$, in the next compact type of complex dimension $8$. All formulas follow by inserting $n=2$ into the preceding definitions and theorems. ::: :::: :::discussion This is the $l=n$, quaternionic-dimension-one family in [[1]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012), §§2–3. The compact-type calculation follows their Theorem 3.9; DS3–DS4 give direct arguments for irreducibility and square-integrability. The ordinary quaternion-valued endpoint is developed in [The Fueter Hardy space](fueter-hardy-space.md), and the section calculation is in [Connections and the Fueter equation](spinor-connection.md). The local [closed pairings](regular-differential-forms.md) lead to separate quotient questions. ::: ## References 1. Heping Liu and Genkai Zhang, [*Realization of quaternionic discrete series on the unit ball in Hᵈ*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfa.2011.12.019), Journal of Functional Analysis **262** (2012), 2979–3005.

wiki/content/quaternionic-analysis/spino.content: --- title: Connections and the Fueter equation description: The nonflat bundle connection, its projected contribution, and the exact scalar weight relating the invariant and flat equations. section: Quaternionic analysis article-kind: exposition order: 5 --- # Connections and the Fueter equation :::discussion The section over the ball has a nonzero connection. After projecting to the first-order spinor operator, that contribution cancels the derivative of one specific scalar weight. This article supplies the calculation used by the representation constructions. ::: ## The equivariant lift Let $G=\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)$. $$ B=\{q\in\mathbb H:|q|<1\},\quad s=1-|q|^2,\quad q=t+ix+jy+kz,\quad K=\operatorname{Sp}(1)\times\operatorname{Sp}(1). $$ Write $e_0=1,e_1=i,e_2=j,e_3=k$, and distinguish the group Lie algebra element $$ \xi_v=\begin{pmatrix}0&v\\\bar v&0\end{pmatrix} $$ from the quaternion $v$. Use $$ \sigma(q)=s^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&q\\\bar q&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V_n=\mathbb C[X,Y]_n,\qquad n\ge1. $$ The polynomial representation and quaternion identification are $$ \tau_n\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}p(X,Y) =p(aX+cY,bX+dY),\qquad T_np=p_X-jp_Y. \tag{L1} $$ Here a quaternion acts through $$ \iota(t+ix+jy+kz)= \begin{pmatrix}t+ix&y+iz\\-y+iz&t-ix\end{pmatrix}. $$ Thus the complex column $(A,B)^t$ represents $A-jB$, and left quaternion multiplication has matrix $\iota(q)$. The first compact factor acts trivially on $V_n$. The lift from a smooth ball spinor to a right-equivariant group function is $$ F(g)=|d|^{-2}\tau_n(d^{-1})f(g\cdot0), \qquad g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}. \tag{L2} $$ For $k=\operatorname{diag}(k_L,k_R)$, the lower-right block of $gk$ is $dk_R$, while $(gk)0=g0$. Substitution into (L2) gives $F(gk)=\tau_n(k_R)^{-1}F(g)$ for $k\in K$. At $g=\sigma(q)$, the lower-right entry is the positive real quaternion $s^{-1/2}$. Since $\tau_n(r)=r^n I$ for real $r>0$, (L2) gives $$ U(q):=F(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2}f(q),\qquad \boxed{f(q)=s^{-(n+2)/2}U(q).} \tag{L3} $$ For a smooth equivariant function $F$, write $(\xi_vF)(g)=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}F(g\exp(\varepsilon\xi_v))\right|_0$. For $n\ge1$ and a smooth right-equivariant $F:G\to V_n$, use the following normalization of the projected first-order operator: $$ 24\mathscr DF=\sum_{v\in\{1,i,j,k\}}vT_n(\xi_vF). $$ The factor $24$ is an operator normalization and does not change its kernel. The projection $v\otimes p\mapsto vT_np$ is $K$-equivariant: the polynomial chain rule intertwines the tangent action $v\mapsto avb^{-1}$ and $p\mapsto\tau_n(b)p$ with the corresponding target action. Consequently $\mathscr D$ is well-defined on the homogeneous bundle and commutes with left translations. ## The nonflat connection ::::proposition SC1 | Connection, curvature, and the changing frame Version: 1 Uses: [Equivariant lift](#equivariant-lift), [operator normalization](#sc-d1). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $U=F\circ\sigma$, the relevant compact connection is $$ A=\frac{d\bar q\,q-\bar q\,dq}{2s},\qquad dA+A\wedge A=-s^{-2}d\bar q\wedge dq. $$ For $C_v=\tfrac12(\bar vq-\bar qv)$ one has $$ (\xi_vF)(\sigma(q))=s\partial_vU+d\tau_n(C_v)U. $$ :::proof Proof of SC1 Direct multiplication, including the derivative of $s^{-1/2}$, gives $$ \sigma^{-1}d\sigma= \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{dq\,\bar q-q\,d\bar q}{2s}&\dfrac{dq}{s}\\[4pt] \dfrac{d\bar q}{s}&\dfrac{d\bar q\,q-\bar q\,dq}{2s} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{L4} $$ The diagonal part is the compact connection of the reductive homogeneous bundle. Its second component, the one acting on $V_n$, is $$ A=\frac{d\bar q\,q-\bar q\,dq}{2s}. \tag{L5} $$ The Maurer–Cartan equation gives its curvature: $$ \boxed{dA+A\wedge A=-\frac{d\bar q\wedge dq}{s^2}\ne0.} \tag{L6} $$ For example at $q=0$, evaluation on $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$ is $-2i$. On $V_n$, $n\ge1$, its action on $X^n$ is $-2inX^n$, also nonzero. Although $A$ vanishes at the origin in this frame, it does not vanish throughout a neighborhood and its curvature does not vanish even at the origin. Consequently a global section, or the fact that the ball is contractible, does not justify replacing covariant derivatives by ordinary derivatives in this frame. A scalar change of frame adds an exact scalar one-form to the connection and does not remove this curvature. The cancellation below occurs only after projection to the particular first-order operator. For a smooth right-K-equivariant $F$, use right differentiation $$ (\xi_vF)(g)=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}F(g\exp(\varepsilon\xi_v))\right|_0. $$ Factor the path through the section: $$ \sigma(q)\exp(\varepsilon\xi_v)=\sigma(q_\varepsilon)k_\varepsilon. $$ Its projection to the ball has derivative $$ q'_0=v-q\bar qv=s v. $$ Evaluating (L4) on that tangent vector, and comparing with the off-diagonal Lie algebra element $\xi_v$, shows that the second compact component satisfies $$ (k'_0)_2=-C_v,\qquad C_v=\tfrac12(\bar vq-\bar qv)=sA(v). $$ Right equivariance therefore contributes the **plus** sign in $$ \boxed{(\xi_vF)(\sigma(q))=s\,\partial_v U(q)+d\tau_n(C_v)U(q).} \tag{L7} $$ Indeed $F(\sigma(q_\varepsilon)k_\varepsilon)=\tau_n((k_\varepsilon)_2^{-1})U(q_\varepsilon)$, whose fibre derivative is $-d\tau_n((k'_0)_2)U$. For explicit comparison in real coordinates: $$ \begin{aligned} C_1&=ix+jy+kz, & C_i&=-it+jz-ky,\\ C_j&=-iz-jt+kx, & C_k&=iy-jx-kt. \end{aligned} $$ The infinitesimal polynomial actions in (L1) are $$ \begin{aligned} d\tau_n(i)&=i(X\partial_X-Y\partial_Y),\\ d\tau_n(j)&=-Y\partial_X+X\partial_Y,\\ d\tau_n(k)&=i(Y\partial_X+X\partial_Y). \end{aligned} \tag{L8} $$ These formulas make the changing-frame contribution completely explicit. ::: :::: ## Projection and cancellation ::::lemma SC2 | The projected connection term Version: 1 Uses: [Equivariant lift](#equivariant-lift), [operator normalization](#sc-d1), [SC1](#sc1). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For every homogeneous $p\in V_n$, $n\ge1$, $$ \sum_vvT_n(d\tau_n(\bar vq)p)=2(n+1)qT_np, \qquad \sum_vvT_n(d\tau_n(C_v)p)=(n+2)qT_np. $$ :::proof Proof of SC2 The cancellation identity in Liu–Zhang Lemma 3.5 becomes $$ \sum_{v\in\{1,i,j,k\}}v\,T_n\bigl(d\tau_n(\bar vq)p\bigr) =2(n+1)qT_np,\qquad p\in V_n. \tag{L9} $$ Here $d\tau_n$ has been extended to all quaternion matrices; in particular $d\tau_n(r)=nrI$ for real scalars $r$. A direct proof avoids any assumption about a flat section. For a complex $2\times2$ matrix $M$, put $$ R_Mp=(M_{11}X+M_{21}Y)p_X+(M_{12}X+M_{22}Y)p_Y, \quad \mathbf T p=\binom{p_X}{p_Y},\quad E=X\partial_X+Y\partial_Y. $$ Expansion of the four matrices $\iota(v)$ gives the differential-operator identity $$ \sum_v\iota(v)\mathbf T\bigl(R_{\iota(\bar vq)}p\bigr) =2\iota(q)(E+2)\mathbf T p. \tag{L10} $$ For example, with $q=\zeta+w j$, the first component is $$ 2\zeta(Xp_{XX}+Yp_{XY}+2p_X) +2w(Xp_{XY}+Yp_{YY}+2p_Y); $$ the second component has coefficients $-\bar w,\bar\zeta$ in place of $\zeta,w$. Since $\mathbf T p$ is homogeneous of degree $n-1$, $E\mathbf T p=(n-1)\mathbf T p$. This proves (L9) for every $n$, not just tested degrees. Now $C_v=\bar vq-\langle v,q\rangle$, so (L9) and $\sum_vv\langle v,q\rangle=q$ give $$ \boxed{\sum_v vT_n(d\tau_n(C_v)p)=(n+2)qT_np.} \tag{L11} $$ Thus the connection term is not zero before weighting, even after projection. ::: :::: ::::theorem SC3 | The section weight identifies the two kernels Version: 1 Uses: [SC1](#sc1), [SC2](#sc2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $n\ge1$, put $U=s^{(n+2)/2}f$. Then $$ 24(\mathscr DF)(\sigma(q))=sD_l(T_nU)+(n+2)qT_nU =s^{(n+4)/2}D_l(T_nf). $$ Thus the lift (L2) identifies the equivariant group kernel with the ordinary Fueter equation for $T_nf$ and proves covariance of the ball action. :::proof Proof of SC3 The weighted cancellation is [[1, Prop. 3.6]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012), with the frame and projection normalized as above. Combining (L7) and (L11) proves $$ \boxed{24(\mathscr DF)(\sigma(q)) =sD_l(T_nU)+(n+2)qT_nU.} \tag{L13} $$ Set $\beta=(n+2)/2$ and $U=s^\beta f$. Since $D_ls=-2q$, the product rule gives $$ \boxed{24(\mathscr DF)(\sigma(q)) =s^{\beta+1}D_l(T_nf)=s^{(n+4)/2}D_l(T_nf).} \tag{L14} $$ The term $-2\beta qT_nf$ from differentiating the scalar weight cancels $(n+2)qT_nf$ exactly. For $n\ge1$, the lift (L2) identifies smooth ball functions with the specified smooth right-K-equivariant functions, and $$ \mathscr DF=0\text{ on }G \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_l\!\left(T_n\bigl(s^{-(n+2)/2}F\circ\sigma\bigr)\right)=0\text{ on }B. \tag{L15} $$ The nonzero factor $s^{(n+4)/2}$ in (L14) gives equivalence on the section. K-equivariance of the projected group operator extends vanishing from the section to all of $G=\sigma(B)K$. This is a smooth differential assertion; it makes no discrete-series claim at $n=1$. Conversely, every smooth right-equivariant $F$ is recovered from its value on the section, since $G=\sigma(B)K$, so the lift is bijective on the specified smooth spaces. Its left translation becomes the ball action in DS-C1. Because the projected operator is left invariant, its kernel and hence the flat Fueter kernel are preserved by that action. ::: :::: ::::corollary SC4 | The discrepancy for any other scalar weight Version: 1 Uses: [SC3](#sc3). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- For $f_\alpha=s^\alpha U$ with any real $\alpha$, $$ 24(\mathscr DF)(\sigma(q))=s^{-\alpha} \left[sD_l(T_nf_\alpha)+(n+2+2\alpha)qT_nf_\alpha\right]. $$ The zeroth-order term disappears exactly at $\alpha=-(n+2)/2$. :::proof Proof of SC4 Insert $U=s^{-\alpha}f_\alpha$ in SC3 and use $D_ls=-2q$. The scalar weight does not flatten the connection: its derivative cancels this particular projected term. ::: :::: ::::proposition SC5 | Direct differentiation of the full lift Version: 1 Uses: [Equivariant lift](#equivariant-lift), [operator normalization](#sc-d1), [SC2](#sc2). Review: pending Formal: none Origin: derivation --- The lift also gives the independent formula $$ (\xi_vF)(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2} \big[s\partial_vf+d\tau_n(\bar vq)f-2(n+1)\langle v,q\rangle f\big]. $$ :::proof Proof of SC5 Put $\beta=(n+2)/2$. To see each contribution, write $$ H_\varepsilon=1+\varepsilon\bar qv+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad b_\varepsilon d_\varepsilon^{-1}=q+\varepsilon s v+O(\varepsilon^2). $$ Then the lift along the right path is $$ F(\sigma(q)e^{\varepsilon\xi_v}) =s^\beta|H_\varepsilon|^{-2}\tau_n(H_\varepsilon^{-1}) f(q+\varepsilon s v+O(\varepsilon^2)). $$ Differentiating yields $$ (\xi_vF)(\sigma(q)) =s^\beta\left[s\partial_vf-d\tau_n(\bar qv)f -2\langle v,q\rangle f\right] =s^\beta\left[s\partial_vf+d\tau_n(\bar vq)f -2(n+1)\langle v,q\rangle f\right]. \tag{L17} $$ The equality uses $\bar qv+\bar vq=2\langle v,q\rangle$ and the scalar degree $n$ action. This agrees with the final derivative display in [[1]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012), printed p. 2991. Applying the projection and (L9) cancels the last two terms, proving (L14) up to the chosen operator normalization. It also agrees with (L7) after substituting $U=s^\beta f$. ::: :::: :::discussion The source of the lift and cancellation is [[1]](#ref-liu-zhang-2012), equation (2.8), Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 3.6. The proof here differentiates the moving frame explicitly. The resulting covariance is used in [the discrete-series construction](fueter-discrete-series.md#ds2) and in [the Hardy endpoint](fueter-hardy-space.md). ::: ## References 1. Heping Liu and Genkai Zhang, [*Realization of quaternionic discrete series on the unit ball in Hᵈ*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfa.2011.12.019), Journal of Functional Analysis **262** (2012), 2979–3005.

# Fueter regular realizations of the quaternionic discrete series

**Later development (2026-10-17):** The [Shimura-style reconstruction](shimura-construction.md) supplies a new linear flat-coefficient two-form, compact and cuspidal cohomology injections, and the precise anti-self-dual weight-two Maxwell correspondence. Earlier open suggestions below are retained as historical stages; they do not describe the current state of these particular questions.

**R060, 2026-10-17.** The central premise of P003 survives. For every integer $n\ge2$, a precisely constrained space of $\mathbb H^n$-valued Fueter-regular functions on the ball is an irreducible unitary discrete-series representation of $\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)$. Its minimal $K$-type is $V_0\boxtimes V_n$. Ordinary single quaternion-valued Fueter functions give the $n=1$ Hardy endpoint, which is unitary and irreducible but not square-integrable as a group representation.

This note gives the corrected construction and proofs of completeness, covariance, unitarity, irreducibility, square-integrability, and the $K$-types. It continues the [connection calculation](liu-zhang-step.md) and replaces the outstanding central representation question in [the initial audit](audit.md). It does not assert the preprint's separate automorphic pairing or coefficient-representation claims. The researcher requested the mathematical reconstruction, not publication of a revised paper; this remains in the research record, outside the wiki.

**Evidence.** The proof below uses the previously derived connection identity, elementary harmonic analysis, and the standard finite-dimensional representation theory of $\operatorname{Sp}(1)$. The $K$-type argument is a detailed reconstruction of Liu–Zhang Theorem 3.9, with the contraction step written explicitly. Their §§3.3–3.4, including Theorem 3.11 and the endpoint discussion, have now been inspected in the [retained full text](../../sources/liu-zhang-quaternionic-discrete-series-2012.pdf), printed pp. 2992–2996. [Exact computations](representation-checks.py) and [output](representation-checks-output.txt) check finite algebraic consequences. This is a supplied proof, not independent review or formal verification. No novelty is claimed for the representation family: the construction identifies the model of Liu–Zhang with the corrected quaternion-valued realization.

## 1. The corrected theorem

Put $G=\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)$, $K=\operatorname{Sp}(1)_L\times\operatorname{Sp}(1)_R$, $B=\{q\in\mathbb H:|q|<1\}$, and $s(q)=1-|q|^2$. All representations and Hilbert spaces below are complex. For quaternion coefficients, the complex scalar acts on the right.

Let $V_n=\mathbb C[X,Y]_n$ with
$$
(\tau_n(M)p)(X,Y)=p(aX+cY,bX+dY),\qquad
M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},
$$
and invariant norm
$$
\left\|\sum_{k=0}^n c_kX^{n-k}Y^k\right\|_n^2
=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{|c_k|^2}{\binom nk}.
$$
A quaternion acts through
$$
\iota(t+ix+jy+kz)=\begin{pmatrix}t+ix&y+iz\\-y+iz&t-ix\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Write a quaternion-valued homogeneous polynomial of auxiliary degree $n-1$ as
$$
h(q;X,Y)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}h_k(q)X^{n-1-k}Y^k=A(q;X,Y)-jB(q;X,Y),
$$
where $A,B$ have complex coefficients. Auxiliary variables commute with quaternion coefficients. Define the fibre
$$
W_n=\{A-jB:A_Y=B_X\}\subset\mathbb H[X,Y]_{n-1}.
\tag{C1}
$$
It has complex dimension $n+1$, embedded in the complex dimension $2n$ space $\mathbb H^n$. The condition is pointwise in $q$ and couples the quaternion components algebraically.

For $n\ge2$, set $C_n=n(n-1)/\pi^2$ and
$$
\mathcal H_n=\left\{h:B\longrightarrow W_n:
D_lh=0,\quad
\|h\|_{\mathcal H_n}^2
=C_n\int_B\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{|h_k(q)|^2}{\binom{n-1}{k}}
 s(q)^{n-2}\,dv(q)<\infty\right\},
\tag{C2}
$$
where $D_l=\partial_t+i\partial_x+j\partial_y+k\partial_z$ acts coefficientwise. The functions in this definition are smooth; equivalently one may impose the equation distributionally in the indicated $L^2$ space.

For $\gamma\in G$, write
$$
\gamma^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad
q'=(aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1},\qquad J=cq+d.
$$
Let $S_m(M)$ be the coefficient-column matrix of $\tau_m(M)$ in descending monomials; in particular $S_1(M)=M$. Regard $h=(h_0,\ldots,h_{n-1})$ as a row. Define
$$
\boxed{(\Pi_n(\gamma)h)(q)
=|J|^{-2}J^{-1}h(q')\,S_{n-1}(\iota(J^{-1}))^t.}
\tag{C3}
$$
The matrix entries multiply quaternion coefficients on the right, while $J^{-1}$ multiplies on the left.

> **Corrected realization theorem, R060/C1/v1.** For every integer $n\ge2$, (C2) is a nonzero complete complex Hilbert space, and (C3) defines a strongly continuous irreducible unitary representation of $G$ belonging to its discrete series. Its compact decomposition is
> $$
> \mathcal H_n\big|_K\simeq\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m=0}^{\infty}V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n},
> $$
> with multiplicity one. The summand $m=0$ consists of constant functions with values in $W_n$ and is the unique minimal $K$-type $V_0\boxtimes V_n$. This is Liu–Zhang's quaternionic discrete series with parameter $l=n$.

The theorem makes no assertion that *all* $\mathbb H^n$-valued regular functions, or arbitrary scalar weights on them, define this representation. The compatibility condition (C1) and the action (C3) are part of the construction.

## 2. An isometric passage to polynomial spinors

Define
$$
\mathcal T_n:V_n\longrightarrow W_n,\qquad
\mathcal T_nf=\frac1n(f_X-jf_Y).
\tag{C4}
$$
This differs from the earlier $T_n$ by the scalar $1/n$, so that it is an isometry. Indeed $f_X/n$ and $f_Y/n$ satisfy the compatibility condition, and for $h=A-jB\in W_n$ the inverse is particularly simple:
$$
\mathcal T_n^{-1}h=XA+YB.
\tag{C5}
$$
Differentiating (C5) and using $A_Y=B_X$ and Euler's identity proves (C4). For a monomial $X^{n-k}Y^k$, the squared norm of $T_n$'s image is
$$
\frac{(n-k)^2}{\binom{n-1}{k}}+
\frac{k^2}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}
=\frac{n^2}{\binom nk},
$$
with absent endpoint terms omitted. Images of distinct monomials are orthogonal for the underlying complex inner product, proving the isometry.

Thus $\mathcal H_n$ is isometric to
$$
\mathcal B_n=\{f\in L^2(B,V_n,d\mu_n):D_l(T_nf)=0\},\qquad
d\mu_n=C_n s^{n-2}dv.
\tag{C6}
$$
The measure is a probability measure, since
$$
\int_Bs^{n-2}dv=2\pi^2\int_0^1r^3(1-r^2)^{n-2}dr
=\frac{\pi^2}{n(n-1)}.
$$
We prove the representation theorem on $\mathcal B_n$ and transfer it through $\mathcal T_n$.

## 3. Completeness and the group action

If $D_l(T_nf)=0$ distributionally, apply $\overline D_l=\partial_t-i\partial_x-j\partial_y-k\partial_z$. Since $\overline D_lD_l=\Delta$ and $T_n$ is a fixed injective linear map, $\Delta f=0$ distributionally. Weyl's lemma gives a smooth harmonic representative. In particular all its coefficient functions are harmonic.

For a convergent sequence in the weighted $L^2$ norm, convergence also holds in $L^2$ on each compact subset, because the weight is strictly positive there. The distributional equation passes to the limit, as does the fixed algebraic fibre constraint. Consequently (C6) is closed and complete. Interior harmonic estimates make evaluation at each point continuous. This also justifies differentiating and averaging its vectors inside the ball.

The polynomial-spinor action is
$$
(\pi_n(\gamma)f)(q)=|J|^{-2}\tau_n(J^{-1})f(q').
\tag{C7}
$$
Quaternion arguments of $\tau_n$ always mean their $\iota$ matrices. The cocycle $J(g_1g_2,q)=J(g_1,g_2q)J(g_2,q)$ proves the group law with the indicated inverse-element convention. The polynomial chain rule shows
$$
\mathcal T_n\pi_n(\gamma)=\Pi_n(\gamma)\mathcal T_n,
$$
including the inverse and transpose in (C3).

For covariance of the differential equation, lift $f$ to
$$
F_f(g)=|d|^{-2}\tau_n(d^{-1})f(g\cdot0),\qquad
g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{C8}
$$
Here the blocks belong to $g$, not its inverse. This is a right-K-equivariant function, $F_f(gk)=\tau_n(k_R)^{-1}F_f(g)$. The [connection proof](liu-zhang-step.md#5-the-corrected-operator-identity) establishes
$$
24(\mathscr DF_f)(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+4)/2}D_l(T_nf),\qquad
F_f(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2}f(q).
\tag{C9}
$$
Left translation on the lifted space commutes with $\mathscr D$, so it preserves the kernel and gives (C7). This accounts for the nonflat connection; no flatness assumption enters.

For unitarity, write $r=|J|$. Then
$$
s(q')=s(q)/r^2,\qquad dv(q')=r^{-8}dv(q),\qquad
\||J|^{-2}\tau_n(J^{-1})v\|^2=r^{-2n-4}\|v\|^2.
$$
These factors cancel exactly against the weight $s^{n-2}$ in the change of variables. Hence (C7), and therefore (C3), are unitary. Strong continuity follows first on compactly supported continuous functions in the ambient weighted $L^2$ space by change of variables, then by density and unitarity; the closed invariant kernel inherits it. Nonzeroness follows from the constant $V_n$-valued functions.

## 4. A direct irreducibility proof

The compact action is
$$
(\pi_n(a,b)f)(q)=\tau_n(b)f(a^{-1}qb).
\tag{C10}
$$
Average over the first factor, with Haar probability measure:
$$
(P_Lf)(q)=\int_{\operatorname{Sp}(1)}f(a^{-1}q)\,da=f(0).
\tag{C11}
$$
For $q\ne0$, this is the spherical mean of the harmonic function $f$ over the sphere of radius $|q|$; for $q=0$ it is immediate. Thus $P_L$ is the orthogonal projection onto the constant $V_n$. The second compact factor acts irreducibly on those constants by $\tau_n$.

Let $M$ be a nonzero closed $G$-invariant subspace. Choose $f\in M$ and a point $p$ with $f(p)\ne0$. Transitivity and the invertible fibre multiplier give a translate $\pi_n(g)f$ nonzero at $0$. Averaging that vector by $P_L$ gives a nonzero constant in $M$. Its second-compact-factor orbit spans the entire constant $V_n$, so $M$ contains every constant.

If $M$ were proper, unitarity would make $M^\perp$ another nonzero closed invariant subspace. The same argument would put all constants in $M^\perp$, a contradiction. Therefore the representation is irreducible. Equivalently, the translates of its constant $V_n$ span a dense subspace.

This proof establishes irreducibility of the whole completed kernel, rather than merely identifying one irreducible subrepresentation inside it.

## 5. An explicit embedding in the regular representation

Fix Haar measure by
$$
\int_G\Phi(g)\,dg=\int_B\int_K\Phi(\sigma(q)k)\,dk\,s(q)^{-4}dv(q),
\qquad \int_Kdk=1
$$
in this disintegration convention. The base measure is invariant. Let $v\in V_n$ be nonzero and $c_v$ its constant function. Use a complex inner product linear in the first argument. Harmonic mean values and the probability measure give
$$
\langle f,c_v\rangle_{\mathcal B_n}=\langle f(0),v\rangle_{V_n}.
$$
The matrix-coefficient map
$$
(\mathcal W_vf)(g)
=\langle\pi_n(g^{-1})f,c_v\rangle
=\langle F_f(g),v\rangle
\tag{C12}
$$
intertwines $\pi_n$ with left translation on functions on $G$.

Schur orthogonality for the finite-dimensional irreducible $\tau_n$ gives
$$
\int_K|\langle\tau_n(k_R)^{-1}u,v\rangle|^2dk
=\frac{\|u\|^2\|v\|^2}{n+1}.
$$
Since $F_f(\sigma(q))=s^{(n+2)/2}f(q)$, we obtain the exact norm identity
$$
\boxed{\|\mathcal W_vf\|_{L^2(G)}^2
=\frac{\|v\|^2}{(n+1)C_n}\,\|f\|_{\mathcal B_n}^2.}
\tag{C13}
$$
Thus a fixed scalar multiple of $\mathcal W_v$ is an isometric embedding with closed invariant image in $L^2(G)$. Together with irreducibility, this proves that $\mathcal B_n$ and $\mathcal H_n$ are discrete series. It removes the need to appeal to an uninspected classification theorem for square-integrability.

For normalized $v$, the inverse constant in (C13) is $n(n^2-1)/\pi^2$ for the specified Haar measure. Its vanishing at the endpoint is consistent with the divergence discussed below; it is not used as a substitute for that argument.

## 6. The compact types and explicit vectors

Let $\mathcal P_{m,n}$ be the degree-$m$ homogeneous polynomials in the real coordinates of $q$, valued in $V_n$, satisfying $D_l(T_nf)=0$. Harmonicity puts this space inside
$$
\mathrm{SH}_m(\mathbb R^4)\otimes V_n
\simeq V_m\boxtimes(V_m\otimes V_n).
$$
Here the scalar spherical harmonics on $S^3\simeq\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ carry the standard left/right type $V_m\boxtimes V_m$.

For the right factor set $R_jf=\partial_{qe_j}f$, where $e_0=1,e_1=i,e_2=j,e_3=k$. On degree-$m$ functions $R_0=mI$. The infinitesimal action is $d\tau_n(e_j)+R_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, so its Casimir is
$$
C_R=-n(n+2)-m(m+2)+2\sum_{j=1}^3d\tau_n(e_j)R_j.
$$
The equation forces the cross term to be $-mn$. To check this without an implicit coordinate change, put $\mathbf Tf=(f_X,f_Y)^t$ and write the flat equation as
$$
\sum_{i=0}^3\iota(e_i)\mathbf T(\partial_if)=0.
$$
Multiply on the left by $\iota(\bar q)$ and contract a column $(A,B)^t$ to $XA+YB$. The result is
$$
0=\sum_i d\tau_n(\bar qe_i)\partial_if
=\sum_{j=0}^3d\tau_n(e_j)R_jf.
\tag{C14}
$$
The last equality follows from $\bar qe_i=\sum_j\langle qe_j,e_i\rangle e_j$. The $j=0$ term is $nmf$, proving the assertion. Consequently $C_R$ acts as
$$
-(m+n)(m+n+2).
$$
The Clebsch–Gordan decomposition of $V_m\otimes V_n$ has distinct Casimir values and contains $V_{m+n}$ once. Hence $\mathcal P_{m,n}$ lies in $V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n}$. It is nonzero: the explicit seed
$$
f_m(q;X,Y)=(t+ix)^mX^n
\tag{C15}
$$
is regular, because $(\partial_t+i\partial_x)(t+ix)^m=0$. Since the candidate compact summand is irreducible and the kernel is $K$-invariant, its nonzero subspace is the whole summand. Thus
$$
\mathcal P_{m,n}=V_m\boxtimes V_{m+n},\qquad
\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathcal P_{m,n}=(m+1)(m+n+1).
$$
Harmonic functions on the ball have homogeneous harmonic expansions. Their degrees are orthogonal on every sphere, and therefore for the radial measure $d\mu_n$. The flat first-order equation holds separately on each homogeneous term. Parseval's identity on spheres and integration in the radius show that partial sums converge in the Hilbert norm. This proves the complete direct-sum decomposition in the theorem.

Under $\mathcal T_n$, the seed becomes the particularly simple quaternion-valued polynomial
$$
h_m(q;X,Y)=(t+ix)^mX^{n-1}.
$$
Its squared norm is
$$
\|h_m\|^2=\frac{m!}{(n+1)_m},\qquad
(n+1)_m=(n+1)(n+2)\cdots(n+m),
\tag{C16}
$$
by the beta integral. Its $K$-orbit spans the entire type of degree $m$. Constants ($m=0$) are the minimal type; the two highest-weight labels increase with $m$, also making this the unique minimum for the usual compact highest-weight norm.

An additional supply of nonpolynomial examples comes directly from translated constants. For any $p\in B$ and $v\in V_n$,
$$
f_{p,v}(q)=s(p)^{(n+2)/2}|1-\bar pq|^{-2}
\tau_n((1-\bar pq)^{-1})v
=\pi_n(\sigma(p))c_v(q).
\tag{C17}
$$
These are regular spinors of norm $\|v\|$, and $\mathcal T_nf_{p,v}$ are corresponding Fueter-regular vectors. Their span is dense by §4. No pointwise product of arbitrary Fueter-regular functions is being assumed regular.

## 7. The first discrete-series member in concrete terms

For $n=2$, write
$$
f=a(q)X^2+2b(q)XY+c(q)Y^2,\qquad
h=\mathcal T_2f=(a-jb)X+(b-jc)Y,
$$
where $a,b,c$ are complex-valued. Thus the representation consists exactly of pairs
$$
(h_0,h_1)=(a-jb,\ b-jc)
$$
that are componentwise Fueter-regular and satisfy
$$
\|h\|^2=\frac2{\pi^2}\int_B(|h_0|^2+|h_1|^2)\,dv<\infty.
$$
The measure is ordinary ball volume, up to normalization. The action is fully explicit:
$$
(\Pi_2(\gamma)h)(q)=|J|^{-2}J^{-1}(h_0(q'),h_1(q'))\iota(J^{-1})^t.
$$
Constant pairs of this form constitute the three-dimensional complex minimal $K$-type. The pair $(t+ix,0)$ is a nonconstant vector, of squared norm $1/3$, in the next compact type of complex dimension $8$. This gives a concrete replacement for the preprint's incorrect minimal-type construction.

## 8. What happens for ordinary quaternion-valued functions

For $n=1$, $W_1=\mathbb H$ and the algebraic constraint is empty. The natural action is the usual conformal Fueter action
$$
(\Pi_1(\gamma)h)(q)=|J|^{-2}J^{-1}h(q').
\tag{C18}
$$
Its multiplier has norm $|J|^{-3}$. The corresponding invariant ball norm would use $s^{-1}dv$, but no nonzero regular function has finite such norm. Indeed its spherical square mean $M(r)$ is nondecreasing, since its components are harmonic and $|h|^2$ is subharmonic. For any nonzero $h$, $M(r_0)>0$ for some $r_0$, so
$$
\int_{r_0}^1\frac{M(r)r^3}{1-r^2}\,dr=\infty.
$$
Instead use the Hardy norm
$$
\|h\|_{\mathrm{Hardy}}^2
=\sup_{0<r<1}\int_{S^3}|h(r\omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\omega),
$$
with normalized boundary area. The boundary Jacobian of the Möbius map is $|J|^{-6}$, exactly matching the squared norm of the multiplier in (C18). This yields a unitary action on boundary values. One can first check it on regular polynomials and their translates, then extend by density; their homogeneous expansion identifies this boundary closure with the displayed Hardy space. The same compact averaging proof gives irreducibility, and the compact types are $V_m\boxtimes V_{m+1}$.

This endpoint is not discrete series. For a constant vector, the lift has size $s^{3/2}$ on the section. Averaging the squared constant-vector matrix coefficient over $K$ leaves a positive constant times $s^3$. Its integral against $s^{-4}dv$ diverges. A discrete-series representation has square-integrable matrix coefficients for these vectors, so this excludes that possibility. Liu–Zhang identify this as their limit $\pi_1$ immediately after Theorem 3.11. The [endpoint follow-up](hardy-endpoint.md) proves the splitting of the normalized spinor principal series at zero into this Hardy space and its Kelvin counterpart, and records the genuine limit-of-discrete-series identification.

Thus the holomorphic analogy is valid at the level of a family of first-order equations and weighted function spaces. In the quaternionic case, the higher members require symmetric spinor values, equivalently the compatible tuples of ordinary Fueter-regular functions above. Changing only the volume weight on unrestricted single quaternion-valued functions does not produce this family with its natural action.

## 9. What is now settled and what remains

The central representation claim has a corrected theorem and proof: the fibre, flat equation, section weight, action, norm, parameter range, irreducibility, group square-integrability, and minimal and higher compact types fit together. The polynomial-spinor space is exactly Liu–Zhang's $\mathcal H_l$ for $l=n$; the map $\mathcal T_n$ supplies the explicit quaternion-valued realization intended by P003. This is not a claim to have classified every discrete series of $G$.

The automorphic part still requires separate work: growth and level conventions, actual examples on quotients, descent of the corrected mixed 3-form, and a valid coefficient bundle replacing the failed finite-dimensional construction. A local closed pairing does not by itself establish a nonzero cohomology class. The question of what additional mathematical insight the quaternionic presentation provides remains a research question, separate from its correctness.

For further examples, the explicit $K$-orbit construction above can replace the preprint's polynomial indexing. The $n=2$ field also suggests comparison with the self-dual Maxwell/spin-one description; that interpretation is recorded as a possible direction, not established here. No new R-node is allocated to these continuations until they warrant a separate investigation.

The 91 finite checks cover the generic contraction identity (C14), full polynomial-kernel dimensions for $1\le n\le4$, $0\le m\le3$, the displayed seeds, probability and seed-norm integrals, the isometry on monomial bases through $n=6$, and endpoint radial divergence. Irreducibility and the closed embedding into $L^2(G)$ are supplied analytic arguments, not conclusions inferred from the finite tests.
